sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Asanga** ​(*asanga*) — ‌Yogacara, ‌Mind-Only · ​Without ​attachment — ​belongs ​to the ​Buddhist ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Yogacara, Mind-Only". ​The ‌name means ​"Without ​attachment"[^1].

**Asanga** ​(c. ​4th–5th century ​CE) ‌is the ​founder ‌of **Yogācāra**, ​the ‌Buddhist school ​that ‌analyzed consciousness ​itself ‌— the ​*ālayavijñāna* ​store-mind, the ‌three natures, ‌the ‌construction of ​the ​world by ‌perception ​— and ​the ‌man who, ​by ​tradition, received ‌the ​future Buddha ‌Maitreya's ​five treatises ​on ​a visit ​to ‌Tuṣita heaven.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical ​scholarly spelling ​**Asanga** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/asanga/). ​The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*asanga* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or ​special encoding ‌is ‌claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Devanagari ​as ​**असन्ग**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"Without ​attachment"[^1].

​The canonical ‌spelling ​**Asanga** ‌matches ​the conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. ​The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*asanga* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no ​lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ‌work ‌is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed ​reference ​spelling, ‌preserve ​capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and ​keep ‌the original ​evidence ​visible. ​The ​displayed ‌form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**a** → ​**A** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **s** ​→ ‌**s** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**n** → ‌**n** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**g** → ​**g** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/asanga/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**asanga** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Asanga.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Asanga" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Asanga" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"asanga" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Asanga ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Asanga ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Asanga ‌place ​yogacara, mind-only ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Asanga appears ‌in ​buddhist ‌tradition as ​yogacara, ​mind-only. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"Without ‌attachment", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Asanga ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Asanga survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Asanga ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Asanga ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌असन्ग, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​yogacara ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Asanga's ​school asks ‌the question ‌most traditions ​bury: not ​'what ​is the ​world?' but ​'**who is ‌building it ​right ​now?**' His ‌answer — ​the mind, ‌constructing its ​world ‌and mistaking ​the construction ​for the ​thing — ​was ​psychology three ‌centuries before ​Augustine and ‌fifteen ​before the ‌laboratory. But ​his founding ‌parable keeps ​the ‌science honest: ​the vision ​came not ‌from analysis ‌but ‌from a ​dying dog, ​and the ‌first act ​of ​the school's ‌founder was ​to bleed ​for a ‌stranger's ​wounds.

There ‌is a ​lesson in ​the pairing. ​Yogācāra's ​map of ‌mind — ‌seeds, stores, ​three natures ‌— ​is as ​intricate as ‌any in ‌antiquity, yet ‌the ‌tradition insists ​it was ‌dictated by ​compassion itself, ​in ​the form ‌of Maitreya. ​Analysis without ​tenderness, ​Asanga's life ‌says, is ​just another ​attachment — ​to ‌being right. ​The name ‌is the ​teaching: **without ‌attachment**, ​even to ‌the map. ‌A psychologist ​who knew ​that ​the last ​obstacle is ‌the theory ‌of the ​obstacle.[^1]
